From Florence, after a «painful» journey, she asks her to send two Sisters.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. My journey, as usual, was painful, for I had a bad headache,1 so that on reaching home I threw myself on the bed in despair.

  2. Listen, as soon as you receive this, send the two sisters, Sr. A. Martina and Sr. A. Stanislaa, here at once; the fare from Pisa to Florence is F. 12.70 for the two.2

  3. Tell Fr Accinelli to buy me one of the cheap chalices and give it to the sisters you are to send. Be as quick as you can; at once, at once.

  4. For your guidance, when I leave I shall let you know two days beforehand.3 I hope those from Piacenza have reached you.4

Goodbye, in haste, your [...]; greet Accinelli for me, and believe me yours

Affect. M. R.

1 As usual. The Mother bore travelling badly.

2 Sr. A. Martina Chigi and Sr. A. Stanislaa Vignoli. The fare for both from Pisa to Florence came to Fr. 12.70.

3 I shall let you know two days before I leave.

4 those: the sisters from Piacenza.

Willing to send the Sisters, she makes some remarks about their number and the service they are to give in the school and possibly in the hospital.

[Dear Mr Mayor,]

  1. I have received your esteemed letter of 27 April. Before sending you the papers Your Lordship requests,2 allow me to make some observations about the said Sisters, which Your Lordship in your wisdom will surely approve.

  2. Having to send three sisters there on a stipend of 1,100 Lire, and not knowing for certain what the Comune3 will give them, this is too little.

  3. Moreover, as I cannot clearly make out from your esteemed letter whether these three Sisters are also to look after the Hospital, this could not possibly be accepted, because the three who teach cannot have duties other than those of the school itself.4

  4. Though sending you 3 at your expense, I would add one more at my own expense, providing them with their bed.

  5. As for the hospital, Your Lordship should know that we have not only the management but also the care and nursing of the sick themselves, doing all the menial work and the cooking; and so in the Hospitals entrusted to us we have only one attendant, who gives the men those services modesty does not allow us; for the rest...

  6. As for teachers, from what I gather from yours, one qualified teacher with a trainee assistant would suffice. Kindly reply as soon as possible,5 as I need to know how to arrange things, having many other requests for other houses. Confident of a kind

reply, I sign myself with every esteem

Humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The date is inferred from the Mayor's reply dated 1 May 1876.

2 Send the papers: prepare the documents requested: qualifications, birth certificates, etc.

3 the Comune: perhaps the Congregation of Charity that ran the hospital.

4 In his reply of 1 May the Mayor explains that two Sisters are enough to teach the girls, as only the first and second classes are involved; the third Sister «should for the present be concerned only with the general supervision of this small hospital and the care of the linen, since at present the hospital itself has two attendants, one for the men and the other for the women».

5 As soon as possible, also because the Mayor wanted the Sisters on the spot within ten days.

Intending to open an institution for the free education of deaf girls, she asks for suitable municipal premises to be made available.

[Most Illustrious Councillors,]

  1. I, the undersigned, placing my trust in the kindness that inspires Your Most Illustrious Lordships, turn to you to obtain a favour that will benefit this city and Province.

  2. It is my intention to open a home2 for Deaf-mute girls, who will be taken in, maintained and educated free of charge; but to carry out this wish I need to find suitable premises, as I have none available for the purpose.

  3. I applied for it to the Honourable Municipal Board,3 to whom I also explained my intention, and was told to turn to Your Most Illustrious Lordships; this I now do, earnestly begging you to grant me free municipal premises for a free home for Deaf-mute girls, leaving it to your wisdom as regards both the education and the healthiness of the place.

  4. The benefit this work will bring, and above all the philanthropy of Your Most Illustrious Lordships, make me hope to obtain what I ask,4 and in this hope I remain

Your Most Illustrious Lordships'

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The letter is undated. It is presumed to belong to this period on the basis of some direct historical evidence: the Cardinal Protector Giuseppe Berardi wrote to M. Rosa on 21.4.1876: «...I am glad to learn that you are opening new houses, among them another in Piacenza itself». AFSA BGpl-1876. Moreover, the Mother was having two Sisters trained at an institute of Religious in Como: Sr. A. Colomba Rimassa and Sr. A. Benigna Mazzini. The former wrote to her on 10.4.76: «...the Director, Fr Serafino... encouraged us in this study so as to give the Bishop the consolation of soon seeing a house for deaf-mutes opened in Piacenza». AFSA D5.

2 Home (ricovero): the name then given to welfare and training institutions.

3 This letter has not been preserved.

4 The reply and other documents on the matter are still missing from the AFSA.

She will send her the «dialogue» as soon as possible. She encourages her to keep up her school work and explains how to manage in the summer.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your little letter and hear what you say about the dialogue; I wrote at once to Onorata to write it and send it to me; as soon as I have it [...].1

  2. Take care of yourself; I hear what a celebration you had in Via Pettinari.2 See, Daughter, how sweet the Lord is! Surely He wants to be loved and served as He deserves.

  3. As for that wretched woman, don't worry, for the Lord knows well how to uncover things; unfortunately He will make her known and she will be put to shame;3 all too soon we see our misdeeds come to light; so courage!

  4. Listen, so as not to have to write again, for I have too much to do, I tell you now what I would like you to do when you have held the June examinations. At the end, as it will be very hot then and it is not wise to keep school, for otherwise you certainly will not hold out,4 it is better to do this: all those at the Fornaci will come to the Parrocchietta and you will go to Rome; then when the others come to Piacenza, if you are not well you will come too.5

  5. And Sr. A. Crocifissa can manage with the others; they can keep the girls occupied and meanwhile teach a little Christian doctrine.6 Do you think I am right? I believe so. Goodbye; I am your Affect. M., who wishes you a thousand blessings, and am

your affect. M. R.

1 She needed the «dialogue» for the end-of-year performance. M. Rosa will have the teacher Onorata Colli write it and will send it as soon as she receives it.

2 On Sunday 30 April Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi had gathered the Sisters of the Rome Communities in Via Pettinari, and they had dined and rejoiced together.

3 It is not known to whom she alludes, as the Sister's letter is missing. Wretched... put to shame: poor thing... will be humiliated.

4 She was in delicate health.

5 She is to proceed thus: all the Sisters of the Via Fornaci school move to the Parrocchietta, you go to Rome, and so you can join the Sisters coming to Piacenza for their vows.

6 Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi and the other Sisters of the Parrocchietta can keep the girls occupied and teach them the catechism.

She sets out the essential conditions for sending the Sisters.

Dear Mr Mayor,

  1. In reply to your esteemed letter of 8 May,1 the agreement is settled for 3 Sisters at 1,700 Lire a year, in addition to everything in the first request.2

  2. For the moment I send you the name of the Qualified Teacher, and that of the Assistant, as I do not have the diploma and other papers here in this house where I am passing through;3 but I shall write at once to have them sent to me, and as soon as I have them I shall forward them to Your Lordship.

Please accept my sentiments of deep esteem

Humble Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Travel paid and only one Diploma.

1 The correspondence had continued, cf. L 188. The Mother's L of 4 May is missing, but the Mayor's of 8 May has been preserved; he restricts the agreement to teaching only, setting aside the hospital service.

2 Cf. L 188,2.

3 Cf. ibid., n. 2.

She advises sending an ailing Sister to Sestri for a change of air. She will go to Ferrara and then return to Piacenza.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours telling me that the newly-weds have arrived in Genoa;1 I wrote to them, addressing the letter to Mamma, that is, to the house in Scurreria.2 So you are truly everyone's refuge; surely they will have been glad to stay, being free to do as they thought best. A pity you are so cramped; if you could see how big it is here! You surely ought not to be so badly off.3

  2. Listen, that sister who was in such poor shape, you know, the one you told me was from Cortemaggiore and whose periods were irregular; I think you might send her to Sestri for a while to see whether she recovers.4 What do you say? Otherwise she will need a change of air while there is still time; write and tell me.5

  3. Listen, I had thought of leaving for Ferrara on Saturday,6 but address your letters to Piacenza, where I am giving orders for them all to be kept for me. And try to go to the blind girls again to see whether the little machines [are] there; otherwise I fear they will forget the little they know.7 Goodbye, dear Daughter; please have them pray, for I am in extreme need. Goodbye, your

Most affect. M. R.

1 The newly-weds: Carlotta and Gaspare Barbiellini. Cf. L 183,8.

2 in Scurreria: in Via Scurreria.

3 You are so cramped: the house was inadequate for the number of Sisters (almost

thirty). Big here = space, cf. L 183,6. Surely you ought not to be so

badly housed for lack of room. They had not yet managed to find

a larger house. Cf. L 24,2; 47,1.

4 That Sister who is unwell, you could send her to Sestri, where the air

is good.

5 Let me know what you have done.

6 Saturday, 13 May.

7 Evidently some blind girls had been taken in at the Sampierdarena

Institute. The superior was to see about obtaining the "little machines"

so that they could practise writing, and so avoid forgetting

what they had learned.

She arranges the transfer of some Sisters. She asks her to buy and send twelve beds. A Sister will arrive from Piacenza bringing the ducks.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, if the sister recovers, keep her, as you say, the one from Cortemaggiore.1 On my orders you will go and fetch Sr. A. Graziosa, Sr. A. Chiara and Sr. A. Federica from the S. P. D'Arena hospital; you will take there the two I sent you last, who were still here, that is, the ones sent, whom I had brought from Piacenza.2 Do you understand? See that you do at once what I tell you.

2. Now I would ask you another big favour: to have twelve iron beds sent to me like yours, with the curtains, that is, the rods for hanging curtains; in short, like the ones you have. Listen, I shall pay you for them little by little; take your time, a year or at least six months; what do you say? But I would like them soon, as soon as possible.3

3. For the rest, I hear that all is going well, and I bless God for it; I shall send you a Sister whom you will send on to the hospital. She will bring you some ducks: 12 are for Mamma,4 and you will take them to her at once; the others are for you. Take them to Mamma at once.

4. So you need no permission to go and see her, because whenever she wishes you may go, and with whomever she wishes. Goodbye, your; tell Fr Accinelli to write to me at once whether he has received my letter dated today. Many greetings to the sisters, and believe me your affect.

M. R.

1 Cf. L ..

2 Sr. A. Graziosa Danieli, Sr. A. Chiara Rossi, Sr. A. Federica Anfossi; cf.

L 194,1; 195,1. You will accompany the two who last arrived there from Piacenza. Cf. L 187,

n. 4. '

3 I would like them as soon as possible.

4 This is Signora Adelaide, M. Rosa's mother.

192,2.

She arranges for a Sister to leave for Ovada and orders her not to send her any food.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you to send Sr. A. Graziosa to Ovada;1 of course it would be better if Fr Antonio could accompany her.2 Meanwhile I am writing to the President; or else, as she has to take the baths, I think she could stay a while in the S. Pier d'Arena house, and so take the baths.3

2. I am sending you the ducklings: 4 for you and 12 for Mamma. Take them to her at once or they will suffer; feed them first.4

3. I forbid you by virtue of holy obedience to send me fish, do you understand? I have orange-flower water to spare. For charity's sake, don't waste money.5

4. Another obedience: I absolutely do not want you to go to the sick. I am sending you this Sr. A. Celeste, who is very dear. For charity's sake, take care of yourself

Goodbye, your Affect. M. R.

1 Sr. A. Graziosa Danieli was being transferred to the hospital community at

Ovada. Cf. L 193,1.

2 It would be better if Fr Antonio Accinelli could accompany her.

3 As she had to take a course of baths, it would be better for her to go first to

Sampierdarena.

4 She is sending the ducklings. Cf. L 192,3.

5 Cf. L 112,1.

She is to take two Sisters to the hospital and hurry the delivery of the beds.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will take Sr. A. Chiara and the one I sent you last, Sr. A. Celeste, to the hospital, and you will take Sr. A. Annunciata,1 at once, as soon as you receive this.

2. I hear they are giving you the beds; now I would like you to tell them I want them for 5 or at the latest 6 June, and earlier if possible.2 Dear daughter, I have a visitation here, and you can imagine how worried I am. I know it is not liked that I leave the beds like this without curtains.3 Try to get them to me.

Goodbye. I am in a hurry, your

Affect. M.

1 Sr. A. Chiara Rossi, Sr. A. Celeste Socci, Sr. A. Annunciata Aliverti.

2 Cf. L 193,2.

3 The curtains round the bed served to screen it off like a cubicle.

She expresses gratitude for his calling the FSA to his Diocese. She accepts his proposal and asks how to arrange the sending of the Sisters.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. The Reverend Missionary Fr Enrico Tipoli has informed me that Your Most Rev. Excellency wishes to have the poor Daughters of Saint Anne in your City;1 and while thanking you for this kindness towards us, I praise God for inspiring it and accept your proposal, assuring you that we shall do our best to make our feeble work beneficial to your Diocesans.

2. We accept the terms2 Your Most Rev. Excellency offers us, trusting in Divine providence, which will not abandon these poor servants of His, who, blessed by Your Excellency, hope to prove worthy of the kindness you show them.

3. I beg you to tell me by letter how I should arrange to send the sisters there, among whom will be the qualified Teacher you desire.3

4. I hope all will go well, and from this we shall conclude that it is the Lord's will for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne to go there and give their very humble service.

5. Meanwhile we are offering special prayers that the Lord may show us His divine will ever more clearly and enable us to be useful to Your Most Rev. Excellency and act according to your wishes.

6. Your Excellency, send us your pastoral blessing, which will protect us on our journey, with a line to tell me how we should arrange to come, and meanwhile I am sure we shall have our travelling expenses paid.4

Bless the least of all, who remains humbly at your feet

Your most devoted Servant Sister ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 Through Fr Enrico Tipoli of the Priests of the Mission she had learned of his wish

to have the FSA at Tropea (CZ).

2 We accept the terms: a rent-free furnished house, an annual payment of L.

600 for two Sisters. Cf. L Mgr. Vaccari AFSA, CvIM.60.

3 For the Bishop's reply cf. L 202.

4 Paid: defrayed.

She gladly takes the opportunity to have her letter delivered to him. She is close to him and interested in his business; she has sent him the linen. She encourages him, urging him to look after his health. Carlotta and Gaspare are at Albaro.

My son,

1. Onorata tells me there is a safe opportunity to send you letters, and I take it at once. Yes, my dear Alessandro, believe that this poor Mother of yours would like an opportunity to write to you every day.

2. I have given the Fr. 40 to the person you told me; just think how I long to hear that you are settled at last, and I am deeply grieved because you are always up in the air, and what is more you are no longer with your cousin.2 Patience!

3. I hope you have received the linen, and the things your uncles sent you to sell, goods and wine. I also saw a magnificent watch.3

4. You see that we all think of you, and it is not true, as you say, that we forget you. No, no! Oh! my God! If you could see how many prayers this poor mother of yours offers, you surely could not entertain the troubling thought that I do not think of you. Oh! My dear Son! One day you will see whether I have thought of you.

5. You ask me about the furniture; your uncles tell me it is not worth it because it costs too much; I sent you the linen at once. I hope you will be able to do something with the goods your uncles sent you.

6. Do not lose heart if something should happen to you on account of your cousin, for you will see that money comes and goes, but the rest, that is health, cannot be recovered. So take care of yourself and remember that everything on this earth comes to an end and only good

and evil remain to us, and these two alone we take with us into eternity; good will win us eternal life, and evil, alas! I cannot even think of it, for it would be a grief that would kill me.4 Shall I never see my dear Son again for all eternity? No, Our Lady will keep him good for me and I shall enjoy him for ever.

7. Your sister is still at Albaro with her husband; I assure you that you have gained a true brother, and when you see him you will be pleased.

8. I assure you I have been left in debt on all sides, but with a little economy I hope to recover and be able to satisfy you too by sending you what you ask; but for now you will surely understand.5 Won't you? So be patient, and I hope you will be pleased with what I have done.

Goodbye, dear son; the Father,6 who is here, sends his greetings, and I embrace you, remaining your

affect. M. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is inferred from the contents and especially from what is said about

Carlotta and Gaspare. Married on 26 April, they had left for Lourdes, had returned

to Genoa on 8 May (cf. L 192,1) and then stayed at Albaro.

2 Alessandro's letter to which the Mother refers is dated 18.4.1876. He

speaks at length about his cousin Emanuele, his bankruptcy and why he is no longer

with him.

3 His uncles Federico and Francesco Gattorno had helped him a great deal, as

the Mother says here. Cf. AFSA. GF1M.

4 Her grief is sharpened by what Alessandro wrote about his cousin: he "is

a freemason".

5 In two letters he had asked her for financial help of 3,000 to 5,000 francs.

6 Father Tornatore.

She sends her two letters to deliver in person.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will receive these two letters;1 take one to Advocate Boccardo, you know, Sr. A. Vincenza's uncle, the one who is to handle the Ricchino lawsuit, and the other is for that judge Arrighetti whom you went to see with Sr. A. Benedetta; Fr Accinelli can show you where they live. Take Boccardo the life of Sr. A. Vincenza2 together with the letter, at once, at once. I think I have made myself clear.

Goodbye, courage, and much more in person

your most affect. M.R.

1 The two letters have not been preserved.

2 The biography compiled by Onorata Colli and published in Piacenza by

Tip. Favari e Breda in 1875. Cf. L 80,3.

She arranges the transfer of two Sisters. She has not yet received everything she asked her to buy.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear you have sent Sr. A. Antonina to the new house.1 Listen, for pity's sake, take her out at once and put in Sr. A. ..., the one who had erysipelas, as the air will do her good; and tell her for charity's sake to be good, do the cooking and try to be exemplary; not to behave like a girl, but always be serious and composed, at home and out of doors.

2. Yesterday I sent you a packet with letters inside and also a life of Sr. A. Vincenza to take to her uncle, Advocate Boccardo.2

3. I hope you have understood: this Sister, Sr. A. Antonina,3 you may send to Sestri for a while to take some baths; meanwhile I also enclose a line for the Superior.

Goodbye, your

Affect. M.

4. I have just received the tartan [cloth], but not the pasta; I hope it

will arrive.

1 The new house. Cf. L 204, n. 2.

2 Cf. L 198.

3 Sr. A. Antonina Gabiotti.

Most Holy Father,

1. As Your Holiness has deigned to grant our poor Institute His Eminence Cardinal Berardi as Protector,1 I make bold to beg Your Holiness that His Eminence may come here to visit the Mother House,2 so that he may see better and become thoroughly imbued with our spirit; and also, for matters of no small importance to the Work, I should like to submit everything to his most wise counsel.

The petitioner, confident of the favour, having kissed the Sacred Foot, prostrates herself with her forehead to the ground

Your Holiness's

Lowliest daughter

Sister A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Card. Giuseppe Berardi had succeeded Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli. Cf.

L 183, n. 3.

2 Beg. Because of his high offices (judge of the Apostolic Camera, mem-

ber of the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, etc.) the Cardinal could not

leave Rome at will. Indeed, to M. Rosa's invitation to come to Piacenza

he had replied that he "depended entirely on the will of the Holy Father" and that

therefore "a request from someone else" was needed. (L to M.R. 21.4.76). On 13

June he told her he would come to Piacenza for the feast of Saint Anne. Cf. AFSA GBpl.
She asks for permission for Cardinal Berardi to come to the Mother House in Piacenza.

Summons to Piacenza, the Mother House, for the Spiritual Exercises.

A.M.F.

Superior,

1. Having decided that all the Superiors are to make the Holy Exercises at the Mother House in Piacenza, I am giving you too timely notice to arrange your House so that everything runs in order during your absence.1

2. Bring with you the half-yearly accounts for 1876, from 1 January to the end of June.

3. Let me know by letter how many religious with you have completed two and three years of vocation.2

4. The purpose of this Circular is for you to be at this Mother House by the 16th of next month.

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 That is, assign to one Sister the task of replacing her in running the

House and give each Sister her duties precisely and clearly.

2 This was to determine the names of the Sisters who would take their vows on the

feast of Saint Anne that year.

She has received his letter and replies that she cannot send only two Sisters, but three. She awaits his word for their departure.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I have just finished reading your most venerated letter.1 God grant that, according to His will, we may give satisfaction to Your Most Rev. Excellency, who so kindly deigns to welcome us into your Diocese; and I pray most fervently to the Lord that all may turn out for the greater good of souls and the sanctification of those to whom this Mission is given.

2. Your Most Rev. Excellency speaks of only two Sisters,2 and this must surely be because I did not explain myself well enough in the letter I sent you. Two Sisters alone cannot form a community; for Your Excellency's sake I can agree to send just Three, with the [hope] of increasing them later.

3. Your Excellency asks me the name of the Qualified Teacher who will come. She is Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini, qualified for 10 years.

4. As for the Rules, we shall bring them when the sisters come, and when Your Most Rev. Excellency has read them, kindly return them. Meanwhile I send you the purpose of our Institution.3

5. As regards our coming, it will take place when Your Most Rev. Excellency thinks fit and lets me know, and I shall be delighted to send you the sisters.4

Deign to grant your Pastoral blessing to the least Servant of the Lord

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The L is dated 30 May 1876 (AFSA CvIM).

2 He speaks quite clearly of two Sisters for the school.

3 Evidently she enclosed a separate summary.

4 The Bishop had specified on this point: "the coming of the Sisters, though most

eagerly desired, could not take place before next October".

Her daughter, a Novice in the Institute, wants to go home. She sends her back, explaining the reasons for her return.

[Dear Madam,]

1. As you will see from your daughter's letter, she absolutely refuses to remain in our Institute any longer, so I must remove her habit and let her return home.

2. Please note that in the two years2 we have had her with us she has always been ill and was no small burden to us, for her illness required much care from doctors, many medicines and very nourishing food; the doctors who treated her can testify [to] this, as can the Paper she herself leaves with us, truthfully attesting what she has received from our poor Institute.

3. Now that she is completely cured she drives us to despair by insisting on leaving and going home, threatening to make a scene if we prevent it. So I am obliged to let her leave for home next Monday.3 Her conduct has always been reprehensible,4 but always excused because of her illness. I believe this is enough without saying more, and I sign myself

Humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 She was the mother of the Novice Sr. A. Marta Fioraghi, of Ferrara. Her name was

taken from the Register of Postulants.

2 The young woman had entered the Institute on 10 April 1874.

3 She drives us to despair, in that she insists arrogantly. She will leave

next Monday, 12 June.

4 Reprehensible: blameworthy.

She invites her to Piacenza for the Superiors' Spiritual Exercises. Directions on founding a new work in Genoa.

A.M.F.

Superior,

1. Having decided that all the Superiors are to make the Holy Exercises at the Mother House in Piacenza,1 I am giving you too timely notice to arrange your House so that all runs in order during your absence.

2. Bring with you the half-yearly accounts for 1876, from 1 January to the end of June.

3. Let me know by letter how many Religious with you have completed two and three years of vocation. These exercises will begin on 16 July.

4. You ask me whom you should appoint as Superior at S. Antonino.2 Sr. A. Elisa provisionally; tell her that after Saint Anne's I shall send her the permanent Superior, as the exercises are on the 16th of that month and it would not be worth her making the journey for so few days.3 You tell me we are to provide the linen; I say no, for I agreed that he must provide everything. Be careful, dear daughter, for otherwise they are all the same, they want to profit at our expense.4

5. The beds have arrived safely and are already set up, as are the chairs, the tartan [cloth] and the lamps.5 Carlotta will not be back for another 5 days; they are both well.

6. As for the other two Sisters, you could take one from Sestri, Sr. A. ..., I don't remember her name, one of the little ones who go begging, a plump one, I think it is Sr. A. Marcellina. If you can manage without them and send them some of your own in Genoa, that will be better,6 all the

more so as now, with summer coming, you will not have so many sick. Do as you think best, your

Most affect. M. R. GATTORNO

1 Cf. L201.

2 At S. Antonino. At the Parish of S. Antonino the FSA were entrusted with

a parish elementary school.

3 You will send Sr. A. Elisa Corsini provisionally. After Saint Anne's the Superior

would go. It was not worth her going earlier for only a few days,

as she had to be in Piacenza from 16 to 26 July for the Spiritual Exercises.

4 The linen for the new house was to be supplied by the parish priest; he must pro-

vide everything. Be careful, for they are all the same, they want to speculate (profit)

to our disadvantage.

5 All the material ordered and sent by her has arrived. The lamps (the two

candelabra) for Carlotta are fine. Cf. L 193,2.

6 If you can manage without them, if you can avoid moving Sisters from other houses

and send some from your own community, that will be better.

She complains of her disobedience in continuing to send fish. She sends some ducks by two Sisters, whom she is to place in the community.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. First of all I must complain, because you have not obeyed me by stopping sending fish and certain trifles; now I tell you that I shall send back the first lot I receive, you may be sure of it, except the pasta, which we have already agreed on.1

2. If a few more copies of the Settimana Religiosa2 could be had, you would do me a great favour, as I badly need them; I have received the books, thank you. As for the Sisters you are to send, I told you: for now Sr. A. Elisa,3 and I shall send one from here, who will hand you this letter and will have some ducks for the M.sa Edvige, Sr. A. Benedetta's sister-in-law. Take them to her at once.

3. I am sending you two sisters; one is for S. P. D'Arena: Sr. A. Atanasia will be for S. P. D'Arena and Sr. A. Ampeglia for S. Antonino.4 The latter is well educated, as is the one going to S. P. d'Arena; for the third you will send Sr. A. Faustina, who can do a little cooking and meanwhile rest a bit; I hope she will have come back from the nuns and they will no longer need her.5 If she should still go to them, we shall put in someone else.

[Dear Mr Mayor,]

1. In reply to your esteemed note of the 3rd inst., I take the liberty of observing that, from the moment you saw fit to entrust the running of your girls' schools and hospital to a Religious Institute, there was no longer any question of invoking the privileges arising from the two articles you cite, whether in favour of the individual teachers or of the Comune.1

2. Yes, I readily understand that a private contract made with an individual is quite a different thing.2

She requests the termination of the Agreement and sets out the serious reasons for this decision.

Most Illustrious President,

1. It is with the greatest regret that I find myself obliged to send you this letter, the chief purpose of which is to declare that I consider dissolved every agreement between my Institution and the Hospital administration made on [6.6.1876], and this on the basis of facts which would not allow us to continue without prejudice to justice, humanity and morality.

2. Though unwell, I left Piacenza to come to the hospital to verify reports that had reached me there, reports suggesting poor treatment of the sick and no better conduct on the part of the Superior I had placed in charge of the nurses.1 To my great surprise I found myself facing a band of enemies who in concert barred my way, perhaps to prevent me from discovering the truth, which could only convince me that the reports were unfortunately true, though I would gladly have refuted them.

3. Your Lordship was no less harsh in receiving me and, when I asked for another meeting, it was kindly granted for the following day; I could not attend because of my poor health, and when it was postponed I was led to hope for the following Thursday. The Management chose to be no less hostile and likewise took pleasure in hindering my inquiry. Then in recent days I sent sisters of mine to speak with the hospital Sisters, and they were turned away without being able to speak to anyone; and the hospital sisters were prevented from communicating with me. What interpretation should I give to such conduct?

4. I shall say it frankly: collusion2 between Administration, Management and Superior. As for having prevented the Sisters of my Institute from speaking with others from the hospital, it is a fine piece of medieval high-handedness,3 which only the courts could deal with; for my part, meanwhile, I must inform you that the Sisters of my Institute have no bond other than that which ties them to the commitment they make towards humanity to assist, nurse and relieve it; and therefore the pressure, the order given them not to communicate with the others, is an arbitrary act for which no name can be found, and against which I protest strongly in the name of justice.

5. I must stop, not wishing to end in a string of accusations in the form of an indictment; just one last word to urge your Administration warmly to consider this matter as soon as possible, to spare greater harm and settle everything in the most conciliatory way still possible.4

6. I likewise earnestly beg that the ban on

communication between the hospital sisters and those

of my other charitable houses be lifted.5

7. As for the manner and time of my sisters' leaving the hospital, it will be agreed jointly, for I certainly do not wish to cause the least harm to the running of the internal administration, which would then harm the poor sick; but I trust provision will be made as soon as possible so that I can withdraw all the sisters.

8. In the hope of seeing this request granted in view of all these unfortunate6 considerations, I have the honour to remain your

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Cf. L 216, 4-5.

2 Abuse of convenience = collusion.

3 medieval high-handedness: an abuse worthy of the Middle Ages.

4 In the most conciliatory, suitable and mutually agreed way.

5 The Sisters of the Sampierdarena and Genoa Community.

6 unfortunate considerations: unpleasant.

Most Illustrious Gentlemen,

1. I send Your Lordships the information you wish to have:1

a) For your hospital the sisters cannot number fewer than five, as a cook, a wardrobe keeper, a portress and two nurses are needed. The wardrobe keeper will of course help the nurses when there are seriously ill patients to watch over, for, as Your Lordships know, we do all the services for the sick, even the lowliest, so that no women servants need be kept, we alone undertaking all the hospital's labours.

b) The stipend to be assigned to each sister is 450 lire; if the Hospital provides oil and firewood, the stipend will be reduced to only 400 lire.

c) As for the maintenance of the sick in all other respects, the following system is used:

The Administration gives the Superior a passbook, or issues vouchers for the butcher, the baker and the grocer. As for other small expenses, the Superior keeps a special register in which she records all the small expenses needed for the sick, such as eggs, ice and so on. At the end of each month this book is checked by the Hospital President, who then gives the Superior a payment order for the sum spent plus an amount as a cash float.2

[Dearest daughters,]

1. Behold, dearest Daughters, by God's mercy we have entered the new year. Two feelings should be awakened in our hearts: one of gratitude and the other of sorrow; gratitude to our heavenly Father for the many blessings He has poured on our Institute throughout the year now ended. A most remarkable grace, worthy of being mentioned first, is His having given us a new Protector in the Person of His Eminence Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi; from the moment this Cardinal took our Institute under his protection, which was at the very beginning of 1876, he has shown himself a truly loving Father.1

2. He has never ceased to give proofs of fatherly love: a most touching proof was the visit he was pleased to make to our Mother House; he made this visit with His Holiness's consent2 and celebrated the feast of the Holy Mother there. The presence of the Cardinal greatly increased the solemnity of that feast, for

it drew a great crowd of distinguished people to venerate the Holy Mother. This visit was a real triumph for our poor Institute. It opened the eyes of many who had paid it no attention; many who had despised it until then changed their contempt into esteem; so this visit was a signal grace the Lord granted us in giving us so great a Protector; and we must pray Him to preserve him for us and enrich him ever more with light and strength for the good of our Institute.

3. What shall we say of the grace the Lord has given us in continuing to the Institute the special goodwill of His Vicar, the Holy Father Pius IX? He showed this special kindness to the Institute by receiving us in audience several times,3 treating us with fatherly cordiality and asking with interest about the Institute's progress.

4. He has a singular affection for our Institute, because our Institute was raised up by the Lord in His Church to honour in a special way that venerable Matron in whose womb the mystery of the Immaculate Conception of Mary was wrought; from the definition of this mystery the Holy Father Pius IX draws that great glory4 by which he shines above all the Popes as the sun outshines the stars.

5. That is why in these early days our Institute has founded and is founding most of its houses in the Pope's state,5 around his Throne, so to speak; for between the Holy Father Pope Pius IX and our Institute there is a secret sympathy, and like a magnet he draws it to himself and wants it to fill his whole state before spreading to other parts of the world; but it is well known that where the Pope's affection goes, there goes the affection of the Bishops and the good faithful.

6. Hence our Lord Bishops, wherever we are, love us and are glad to have us; so too the faithful: they appreciate our services, and very many sick people of every condition ask for our care, both at home and in hospital.

7. Meanwhile, in a hospital which, through the malice of wicked people, we had to leave against our will, although they used every possible means to make us stay, and from which we keep receiving requests to return, the sick weep at no longer having our care, and their tears are joined by those of the good people of that City.6

8. Our schools are very numerous,7 and the Lord blesses them through the Holy Mother's intercession, and the girls make progress there both in virtue and in learning. In this new year, now that

we have arranged that in all of them the joy the Holy Mother felt in the Immaculate Conception of Mary be honoured with three Our Fathers, Hail Marys and Glory Bes, which are like the badge distinguishing our schools from those of other Institutes, the blessings will be more abundant.

9. We had a testimony of the affection Bishops and

peoples have for us in the year just ended; in it the Institute grew

prodigiously both in foundations and in members: we

founded nine Houses8 and clothed 76 sisters, and

4 died.

10. See how strong and numerous are the reasons we have, dearest Daughters, to bless and thank the Lord. But have we responded to so many graces? On the whole, by God's grace, the Sisters fulfil the purpose of their vocation, which is to imitate the Holy Mother by keeping the Rules and to honour her prerogatives, especially that of being Mother of the Immaculate; we pay her this honour by reciting at the appointed times the Institute's ejaculatory prayer: blessed be our glorious Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate,9 and reciting it fervently, because it contains a profession of faith by which we believe that Mary, in the womb of our Holy Mother, at the first instant of her conception, was conceived immaculate, that is, without original stain. And since this prayer is almost continuous from morning to night, through it the Institute makes, as it were, a continuous act of faith in the Immaculate Conception of Mary.

11. This imitation of the Holy Mother and this veneration of her prerogatives is the work God wants of us as Daughters of Saint Anne, as a testimony that we love Him. And so it can be said that the Sisters on the whole love the Lord with all their hearts, but it is not true of all that in the past year they were faithful in imitating and venerating the Holy Mother in the way explained.

12. We shall mention some faults into which they have fallen; one, noticed even by outsiders, was poor behaviour in the street. The bearing of the Daughters of Saint Anne in the street should be both natural and modest.10 Now it was observed that some walked with their heads bent too low and their necks twisted, swaying right and left, bumping into each other as they walked and walking too far apart. These lack ease of manner; others went to the opposite extreme, I mean they raised their eyes to the windows, turned towards the shops on right and left, and cast their eyes

into carriages. This is a fault of worldly boldness, contrary to the modesty a Daughter of Saint Anne should have. There were some who talked, gesticulated and laughed in the street, something utterly contrary to the absolute silence the Rule requires in the streets of towns and villages.

13. Likewise in some we had to deplore the fault of leaving their companion in the sick person's house and going out of the room alone to talk to the household;11 these faults are so ruinous for the Institute that those who have committed them [must in any case correct themselves].

14. Some were lazy in the morning, not rising promptly at five at the sound of the bell; or for some slight ailment, of head or stomach or whatever, did not go to meditation or went late, and did so without the Superior's permission; others likewise were not prompt in attending all the community exercises, prayers, breakfast, dinner, supper and recreation.12

15. This, sisters, is the cause of sorrow and tears for some of you: these, sisters, are the faults from which the Institute must be cleansed in some of its members in this year of '77 now begun; the Lord asks this amendment in gratitude for having mercifully waited for us until this new year; the Holy Mother, who keeps us in her family, asks it; our neighbours ask it, for they can hope for nothing good from lax Sisters, indeed will only be badly edified by them; and finally, if we do not amend, we shall not be admitted to share the glory enjoyed by the Holy Mother and, with her, by those Sisters who lived here below full of the spirit of their vocation. May our God grant us all these graces, as we pray Him with all our hearts.

16. To our great displeasure we have found the accounts of all the houses inaccurate. The Superiors will have to take new measures about this. We remain your

She asks her to send a good supply of candles to the Piacenza House. She encloses money to buy what is needed for Alessandro, who is ill.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to ask you kindly to send some candles to the Piacenza house, as they have run out; please do, the Bishop is to go there and they have no candles.1

2. Tell me something about Ricchino.2 Listen, I enclose 6 [francs] for Alessandro;3 buy him a chicken or two and whatever you see he most wants.

3. If the sister eats at the aunt's house, for charity's sake I would not want her to be a burden, do you understand?4

4. I am glad he is better, but I wish he would behave a little better. Goodbye, your [M. R.].

Give him my love; tell him to behave and go home as soon as possible, or he will come to a bad end. Goodbye, it is late

your affect. M. R.

1 The Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr. Giovanni Battista Scalabrini.

2 In the letter of 12 January which the Mother is answering, Sr. A. Santina speaks of

3 In the same letter she gave her news of Alessandro's illness.

She again asks for the 1876 accounts and sends her a draft letter.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I had someone write and ask you for the 1876 accounts: what are you doing? Everyone sends them to me except you.1 I also had them tell you to try to send me something by registered letter.2

2. I am sending you the letter for Signora Marianna.3 Goodbye, I am in a hurry; be sure to treat Fr Tito4 well and give him my warm regards; I am expecting him in Rome.

Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 She has already written to her about it: cf. L 280,7.

2 In the same letter she asked her to send the cash surplus.

3 Signora Marianna, the Director's housekeeper.

4 Fr Tito Borgatta, a member of the Congregation of Charity at Ovada. He took

an interest in the good running of the hospital and helped the Sisters by advising them

on their nursing service.

To a Sister who asked to go to her dying brother she answers no. She too had to offer such a renunciation at the deaths of her father and brother, and recently could not go to her son, who was gravely ill.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line in reply to your telegram. Listen, my Daughter, if it were your father or mother, then yes, it would be granted; but a brother, this has never been allowed in 11 years.2

2. My [brother] died, my Father died, and for God's Work I sacrificed seeing them; when I left my father they said he had only a few days to live, and I bade him a last farewell and left for Rome. I had hardly arrived when a telegram came: Father dying, and in the evening he died! The Work required me to be at my post to put in order what had to be done.3 So it was with my brother.4

3. Daughter, before answering you I prayed much in the chapel at the feet of my God,5 where I was told again and again to write to you in this way.

4. So join me at the feet of our Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament6 and hand your brother over to Him, and with a fervent heart leave him in His heart. Ah! you will see that this visit will do him more good than your presence. Courage! Jesus wants sacrifices from His Spouses; this is how He tests them. Blessed are you if you know how to sacrifice everything for Jesus with resignation.

5. Do you want another proof? Last night the latest letter came from an aunt of mine,7 telling me that Alessandro is a little better, that

in these days he was close to death, and I had already made a sacrifice of it to God.

6. He is my son! The pain of this you cannot know; it is a mortal agony. There were moments when I felt my soul tearing away from my body! Ah! what pain! My God, I would never have believed one could suffer such cruel torment in this world. I am a Mother! I left them to serve God! but I am a Mother! I tell you!8 Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 The addressee is unknown. The name is missing from the letter and there are no documents

that might identify her.

2 Since the Institute began it has never been granted to anyone.

3 Her father died on 27 January 1874, while M. Rosa was in Rome busy

reorganising the Institute's four houses.

4 Her brother Emanuele had died on 7 February 1873. At that time the Mother

was also in Rome.

5 prayed much. She took decisions great and small in prayer,

letting herself be enlightened by the Holy Spirit.

6 Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament.

7 Aunt Emilia, her mother's sister. Cf. L 284, n. 4.

8 Words of striking simplicity and evocative power.

She has received the statement of accounts and the money. She thanks and blesses her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste because I am extremely busy; we are moving house;1 I leave you to imagine how tired I am these days.

2. I have received your letter with F. 125 inside. Thank you; it came just in time; it was a bad moment, I had nothing and had to pay F. 300. Oh! it arrived! God be blessed!

3. You will have received my other letter with the reply you are to give Marianna.2 The accounts are in order.

Goodbye; many greetings to the sisters, and receive a thousand blessings from your affect.

M. R.

1 They were moving to the house at Vicolo Margana 12.

2 Cf. L 285,2 and 280,1.

She asks for news. Advice about the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received the cabbages, and the butter and eggs, from the sisters. Thank you very much.

2. I want to know how the Uppello house is going. You tell me to take away the sisters you don't need;1 and how can that be done? Must I keep them all myself?

3. Listen, Sr. A. Carolina is for S. Martinello.2 As soon as she has recovered from her cough (please keep her in bed), she must go there at once: that is what we agreed. Do you understand? The others could not be better off than at Foligno.3

4. Be a little patient; it is true I would not have sent you Sr. A. Marziale;4 be patient, I shall soon change her.

Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 There were a few more sisters in the community than needed. The Mother kept them

there because of the good climate, as their health was rather

poor.

2 Sr. A. Carolina Rusca (cf. L 277, n. 1) was assigned to S. Martinello.

3 Better than at Foligno. Besides the good climate, there was the good superior Guglielma,

who knew how to care for the Sisters.

4 Sr. A. Marziale Mola. She was unwell and needed expensive treatment.

She says she is ready to sign Signora Anna Micheletti's power of attorney at once.

Reverend Parish Priest,

1. I have received your esteemed letter together with the two lines from Signora Anna Micheletti.1 Very sorry that I cannot send my secretary, as she is not well, I beg you, most worthy Parish Priest, to come here with Signora Micheletti's power of attorney.2

2. Nothing need be forced; as soon as I am told to sign I am quite ready; no one has deceived or wishes to deceive;3 bring the deed drawn up and I shall sign it at once.

My respects to Signora Anna, and a thousand greetings to you from

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The lady had put her large house at Cascina

(Pisa) at the disposal of the FSA, so that they could teach the "children of the people" and give her

the care she needed.

2 ...with the power of attorney. She wanted the relevant legal deed of power

of attorney to be completed.

3 The lady feared that the deed would not be signed.

The house move is under way.

A.M.F.

[My daughter,]

1. There is an enormous amount to do; the house move1 is under way; I hope it will be finished on Saturday and on Sunday2 we can put everything in good order, and then I shall send word of the day the girls are to come.3 Goodbye; many greetings to the superior, and I am your

affect. M. R.

1 She was organising the new house at Vicolo Margana 12. Cf. L 283, 291.

2 Sunday 28 January.

3 the boarding girls.

She encloses a letter to be delivered to a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Get the enclosed letter to Sr. A. Elisa at once.1 I have received the basket; Carla thanks you and Gaspare will write to you.2

2. My address: Vicolo Margana No. 12.3

3. It is late; I am dog-tired. Goodbye, your affect.

M. R. You will see what a lovely little house it is.4

1 She was to have it delivered to Sr. A. Elisa Corsini.

2 Carla and Gaspare: her daughter and son-in-law.

3 This is the new house. Cf. L 290.

4 She means the house mentioned above.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I could not read yours, so I answered what the man told me.1 Listen, do stay on; I am more than pleased, because then the girls will find everything here2 in order and will have a fine school when it is finished, and the refectory too.

2. Now I would like you to set the girls to work sewing those things for the seminary, otherwise there will be serious trouble with those who want them. Listen, see that it is well sewn, you know.

3. Goodbye; I shall tell you something very lovely in person, lovely; a giant's courage, that is how one becomes a good officer.3

Your

most affect. M.R.

1 She answered orally what the bearer of her letter told her.

2 She urges her to stay on, she is better pleased, and explains why: the

girls will find everything ready here, that is, in the Vicolo Margana house.

3 ...something very lovely: the opening of a new house at Maratea. That is why she

encourages her. She will be the one to go there and start the work.
She is to stay on with the girls and set them to work; she will let her know about their move later.

Surprised at what she has written, she assures her that she has not spoken ill of her. She will go on remembering her in prayer.

Jesus be always with us. Dear Madam,

1. Last night I received your postcard and was surprised at what it contained.1 Believe me, not out of goodness or even virtue, but simply by habit,2 I can assure you that I have never been in the way of speaking ill of my neighbour, certainly not; and the very Archbishops you name3 can vouch for what I say.

2. With one I never had the good fortune to speak;4 with the other, of Florence, what I said was in praise of you and in charity for your sufferings, for which I always pray and shall pray that the Lord may grant your wishes.

Meanwhile do not forget one who has the pleasure of remaining your unworthy poor

Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO, Vicolo Margana No. 12

1 The postcard has not been preserved. Its contents are inferred from what

the Mother says to her.

2 simply by habit: as a personal rule of conduct.

3 the very Archbishops: Mgr. Micaleff of Pisa and Mgr. Eugenio Cecconi of

Florence.

4 With one: she never spoke with Micaleff. She writes to him, cf. L 294.

She informs him of the withdrawal of the Sisters from Cascina and explains why.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. It would have been my duty to let Your Most Rev. Excellency know that our sisters are no longer in your Diocese.1 With real regret I had to withdraw them;2 I shall not dwell on the reason, as Your Excellency will already have been informed by the good lawyer Barsali.3

2. Believe me, Most Rev. Excellency, I did all that was humanly possible, as did the poor Sisters, but for all that we did not succeed.4 God has His purposes, and they are inscrutable!! So may His Divine Will be done in all things.

3. I take the liberty of copying for you, in strict confidence, the last note the lady wrote me in her own hand, leaving aside a letter received earlier, half written by the Parish Priest and half by her, which is something too!!,5 in which I was threatened that if I persisted in refusing to dissolve the contract, serious steps would be taken.

4. Most Rev. Excellency, she had only to express a wish and it would have been granted at once. Granting that pressure was put on her, though for several months she had been insisting that we go there for this donation, the only thing done was that after five days in her house I told her I was leaving,6 seeing that nothing was being done; and I said the same to lawyer Barsali, telling him that I could not (for reasons of the Work) stay longer; as I could not see her, a note was written to her.7

5. It must have been God's permission; my only regret is having had to leave a Diocese where the Pastor welcomed and blessed us with such charity.

6. Deign therefore to grant this wretched servant

of the Lord your Pastoral Blessing, while at your feet, full of veneration, she remains Your Most Rev. Excellency's

Humble Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

7. P.S. Here is the note:8 She warns that if she should be accused also before the Bishops of Florence and Pisa, by simply setting out the facts with the documents in hand she will know how to obtain justice. That accursed spring of self-interest, which made an Apostle a traitor and a reprobate, has ruined a work prepared for many years with so much toil and trouble, pain and sacrifice; yes, out of sheer self-interest they wanted to make a work which she wanted to be a work of Providence. As for the rest!

Anna Micheletti

1 In your Diocese: at Cascina.

2 I had to withdraw the Sisters from the Diocese.

3 Signora Micheletti's lawyer, Giuseppe Barsali, had conducted the

negotiations from the start, explaining the lady's plan to M. Rosa.

4 we did not succeed. It was impossible to satisfy the lady, who

was very demanding and wanted the Sisters to devote themselves solely

to her service and not to the school, as had been agreed. Cf. the Sisters' letters:

AFSA, CsIC, D6.

5 leaving aside... something!! omitting a letter received, written in the first

half by the Parish Priest and in the other by her...

6 Granting... I was leaving. I admit that pressure (oppression) was put on her,

since for several months she herself had insisted that we go to Cascina for this

donation; the only thing she can perhaps reproach me for is this:

after five days in her house I told her I was leaving,

since nothing was being settled.

7 As it was not possible to see her in person, I wrote her a note.

8 She copies for him the note she received, mentioned above. The Mother had re-

plied to this note. Cf. L 293.

She wants to know whether a Sister has been sent to S. Martinello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I would like to know whether you have sent the Sister to S. Martinello yet.2 If you need her and no longer want to send her, write to me at once and I shall send another; tell the Superior everything she is to do at Uppello, and the duchess too.3

Goodbye; I am so busy that [...]. Goodbye, no more.4

Your Affect. M. R.

1 The letter is marked 1/1877, that is, 1 January, but it is certain-

ly from February because of its close link with the following L 297.

2 Sr. A. Carolina Rusca was to go to S. Martinello. Cf. L 288,3.

3 You will explain to the new Superior of Uppello what she is to do; you will speak of this

also to Duchess Agnese di Sora.

She answers some questions about the School and asks her to send six pullets.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am so busy I have no time to breathe. You ask whether I have seen the Priest. Yes, I spoke with him and he gave me the best possible news of you.

2. You ask about taking on the other school for older girls as well;2 no, no, because moderation is needed in everything. Be moderate and you will last; so the schools you have are enough and nothing more;2 you did well with the sister;3 so try to keep strong and full of courage.

3. Carla is still up and about, and until she is well I cannot move; meanwhile the fine season will come and the lame will go out.4 Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

4. Carla will be taking to her bed any moment;5 I would like you to send six

pullets, and I shall be grateful for the favour.

Goodbye. She is here and sends you her greetings.

1 The Sister had asked her what to do, as many older girls

wanted lessons on Thursdays from 10 to 11.

2 It is good, says the Mother, to set limits to the already heavy commitments she had

in the school.

3 She had admonished a sister to behave differently.

4 The lame: those who limp will go out.

5 Carlotta was expecting a child and was in the eighth month of pregnancy.

She is to keep Sr. A. Carolina and also the extra Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to tell you to keep Sr. A. Carolina,1 but you must be patient, and keep the others too for a while.2 As soon as I can I shall take them away, but for now we need a little patience. Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

Vicolo Margana no. 12.

1 On the Sister's departure, cf. L 288 and 295. 2 Cf. L 288,3.

She explains how to deal with a Sister who is leaving the Institute.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Everything you have done is fine; go and accompany Sr. A. Enrichetta, but see that her habit is removed and dress her as a laywoman.1 Do you understand? I am also writing to the Father to send you the papers,2 but it would be good for you to leave as soon as you receive this, and I shall send you the money and papers afterwards. I shall send the money to you and the papers to the sister; but she should pay for the journey, as she is leaving by her own choice.

2. Do you understand? In any case, if you can get it for the moment, borrow it and the Father will send it to you later. So I order you to remove her habit.

3. As for your niece, I am delighted; but you alone know that we cannot go to our relatives' homes alone; but please do not stay, as this is such an exceptional case; I beg you.

Goodbye; this is my order. Your

Affect. M. R.

P.S. May the Lord bless the Sister and let her find peace where she is going.

1 Sr. A. Enrichetta Salvatelli had asked the nuns of Urbino to be admitted

to their monastery and had received a favourable reply. Cf. L Sr. A. Predicanda

Romano to M. Rosa of 12.1.1877.

2 Fr Tornatore was to send her the documents from Piacenza.

She urges her to avoid overworking the nursing Sisters. She is to have the Sisters ready for Bordighera and prepare them by having them learn French.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. You say you fear I do not receive your letters; I tell you I receive them all; I fear it is the other way round, because I wrote to you in my own hand and you did not answer what I asked.

2. Now I hear that the poor nurses are going out every night;1 mind they don't all end up chronic invalids; it does not even seem orderly to me. For 8 or 10 days once in a while it can be done, but they will hardly stand it continually, and then things will not go well.2

3. I am always very worried about those in Genoa, always afraid of how things are; I assure you I always see things black!

4. As for those who are to leave for Bordighera, for the moment they stay put,3 but keep them ready, for it will be at any moment; they telegraphed to wait a little longer, as the house is not yet ready and the furniture is lacking.

5. If meanwhile a young teacher could be found to teach them a little French (those in Piacenza are already learning it), you too could have them learn a bit, even if they make mistakes, as long as they can make themselves understood; and then, being there where all the foreigners speak it, they would improve.4 Hear what Accinelli says.5

6. Goodbye; I am in such a hurry; I am both the donkey and the master, and so

I think that when I can go on no longer I shall throw down the load and go to my blessed rest.6 Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 As there were so many patients to nurse, the Sisters were on

duty several nights in a row.

2 The Mother disapproves, first for the Sisters' health and then for the

lack of organisation in sharing out the work.

3 As for those... stay put. Those who are to leave for the new house at Bordi-

ghera are to stay put for the moment.

4 A knowledge of French was needed especially for nursing

"foreign" patients, who went there for their health.

5 Fr Antonio Accinelli was a most trusted spiritual and admin-

istrative adviser.

6 She did not confine herself to directing. She worked with head and hands to set

up house. Cf. L 287,1; 291,3.

To the Sister who has lost her mother she explains the demands of following Jesus in religious life.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear of your grief at losing an earthly mother. Listen, I left Genoa, where I was told plainly that my father had only a few days to live; indeed, when I reached Rome, after travelling without a break, he died!1 The Work required me to leave, and I did so promptly. Another [sacrifice]: of son and mother, and brother too.2

2. God, my daughter, is greatly pleased by sacrifice, and the Lord, our master, said to Peter: "Leave father and mother and follow me";3 and [to the one who said to Him:] I am going to bury him, the Lord replied: [let] the dead bury the dead, and did not allow him.4 So what does this mean? That once we have given ourselves to Him, He does not want us to have dealings with earthly things any more, but to raise our minds to Him alone: He becomes jealous. Courage, pray, and nothing more.5

3. I would like to tell you a million things more, but if you knew that I have not a moment to breathe and am stealing this quarter of an hour for you! So I would like these words of mine to suit you6 and bear real fruit in you.

Goodbye; greet everyone for me. I am your

affect. M. R.

1 She shares her daughter's grief by telling of her own experience. She has also spoken of her father's death to another Sister. Cf. L 286,2.

2 In the same letter she speaks of her brother and son. Cf. ibid. note 4 and par. 5-6.

3 Cf. Mk 4:16-20. The Mother quotes the Gospel freely.

4 another of the disciples said to him: "Lord, let me first go and

bury my father". But Jesus answered him: "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own

dead" (Mt 8:21-22).

5 The essence of the following accepted and professed is here: Him alone. To raise

our minds to God in prayer, which is desire, a seeking for Him alone.

6 suit you: be appropriate.

She asks her to send the three Sisters to the new work at Bordighera and provide them with personal clothing.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, Sr. A. Giovannina will arrive on her way to Bordighera; give her the Sister you tell me does so well, Sr. A. Caritas, and the other, Sr. A. Redentore; they will leave on Monday1 by the 7 o'clock train to be at Bordighera by 12.

2. Please see that they are very neat, with a nice clean veil, habit and shoes, because a Countess will meet them at the station and take them to her house.

3. For charity's sake, my daughter, you know well that first impressions count, so I rely on you. If they lack anything, buy it for them.2 See that the collar3 is clean and fits properly, for I am very anxious, but I trust in you, who know well what ladies are like.

4. So be careful; then write and tell me everything; and also mind they don't miss the train, but are ready.

Goodbye

your affect. M. R.

1 The first three Sisters of the work begun at Bordighera, nursing

the sick at home: Sr. A. Giovannina Pizzorno, Sr. A. Caritas Tornali and Sr. A.

Redentore Bassarini, left on 19 February.

2 Buy them everything they need.

3 the collar: the starched collar must be clean and the right size.

She allows her to be confirmation sponsor for a young lady. She is pleased with the news about night nursing.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Now you won't say I write to you too little: every day, always... You ask whether you may be confirmation sponsor for that lady; I say yes, indeed it is a holy work and I am glad.1

2. I am also delighted because you tell me the nurses now lose only one night.2 Blessed be God, who knows how to make everything turn to our good!

3. You cannot believe how it pained me, for I saw that in time the spirit would have been lost.3

4. Yesterday Gaspare4 asked me whether you remember the stockings you promised him, and he hopes you will bring them when you come to Rome.

Goodbye, I am in a hurry,

your affect. M. R.

1 Nothing is known of the confirmand for whom Sr. A. Santina was

sponsor.

2 Lose only one night. They do night watches at intervals, wher-

eas before night duty went on for many nights in a row.

Cf. L 299, 2-3.

3 The spirit lost. Watching at night, the Sisters had to sleep by day,

to the detriment of an orderly life of fraternal communion and prayer.

4 Gaspare Barbiellini Amidei, Carlotta's husband.

To start negotiations on employing the working girls in his factory, she asks for a draft contract.

[Dear Sir,]

1. Last night I received your esteemed letter,1 which I read with real pleasure; God bless you, you are already counted among our distinguished benefactors. Your kindness, so fully expressed in this letter, prevents me from drawing up a contract, as it would seem too bold and indelicate of me in the face of such fine hopes for our poor girls.2

2. Let us do this: Your Lordship draws up the contract and then sends me a copy; if nothing in it conflicts with our Constitutions, as regards the maintenance of both Sisters and girls, I shall sign it; otherwise I shall make those observations which Your Lordship will surely see are a matter of sheer necessity; what do you say?

3. As for sending persons fit to serve you and ensure the smooth running of your factory, I shall see to that myself, and I hope, with God's help, we shall succeed as you wish.

4. I eagerly await your reply, and ask you to give my respects to your excellent sister,3 while I remain, with great esteem, Your Lordship's

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The L is dated 17 February.

2 Marchetti says he is most willing to take the working girls and "Sisters

as directors".

3 Sr. A. Mercede Massimelli had gone to Cremia and met Marchetti's sister. In the said L the industrialist states: "I am sure that Rev. Sister A. Mercede, in explaining my intentions regarding the new organisation of this silk factory, will also have told you of my commitments to the present workers".

She thanks him for his concern for the community. She deplores the scandal given by a Sister who dressed as a priest.

[Most Reverend Archpriest,]

1. Deeply sorry for your distress, I thank you at the same time for the care you always show for our poor House there. God reward you.

2. The incident Your Reverence describes1 concerning poor Sr. A. Panasia is dreadful!! It is far more deplorable on the part of the wretched Superior,2 who after so horrible an incident did not know how to correct her subject severely and write to me, so that I could have remedied it.

3. She is even more to blame for allowing her to put on the clothes and go out. I do not condemn the subject, but I weep over the Superior's fault.

4. I am told that when this wretched sister was wearing the priest's clothes, the Superior laughed and they all made a racket;3 and by taking part in something (which, most worthy Archpriest, [is] so dreadful) this Superior made herself more guilty than her subject.

5. I assure you that what I write was not reported by Panasia but by other people. She certainly did not write ill of herself to me.

6. My God, going out into the square, Archpriest, is a knife plunged into my soul and I feel torn apart. Oh! my Jesus, what a scandal, how His Heart must have suffered!! My God, have pity on a creature who...4

Bless me and believe me ever your most unworthy servant

Sister A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The L referred to is missing from Fr Tamagni's correspondence.

2 At Carnival Sr. A. Panasia Bellardo had dressed up wearing

a priest's clothes. The Mother deplores what the Sister did, but considers

the Superior even more blameworthy (wretched).

3 made a racket: shrieked.

4 She does not finish the sentence.

Your affect. M. R.

My daughter,

2. Thank you for the money. The Lord bless you. Goodbye, ever your

She sets out the contract terms of the previous silk factory. She begs him to send for the girls soon, as they have already been dismissed and need work.

Dear Sir,

1. I reply by return of post to your esteemed and kind letter. My God! How can I, Your most wretched servant, thank You enough for giving me a new benefactor, so charitable and kind to me, so unworthy a creature!! With what words can I express my gratitude to Your Lordship? I would go on too long if I tried to say what gratitude dictates. I shall only assure you that you will never be forgotten by the poor Daughters of Saint Anne; they will remember you for ever.

2. Here is what has been the rule in the other factories where the Daughters of Saint Anne are.1 The manufacturer binds himself by the year, and the number of years is fixed by mutual agreement; then the number of sisters needed for management, both supervision and teaching, kitchen, housekeeping, all to us, and the linen room.2 As there are many of them, the said sisters' stipend will be set at fr. 300 a year, including firewood and oil both for lighting and cooking.

3. The girls. If the manufacturer wishes to maintain them, food is reckoned at 6.50 a day each,3 and a calculation is made for clothing according to the number: for sixty it is fr. 100 a month;4 the sum increases from there according to the number of girls entrusted to us.

4. These are the points5 of the contract to be made, if Your Lordship finds them to your liking. The other conditions are as in all other contracts: that neither party may terminate except after three years or more, giving

6 months' notice; that this may happen only for just reasons; let the reasons be stated.

5. Enough, I do not wish to add more; Your Lordship will draw up the rest.

6. I only beg, I implore you to send for them as soon as possible, even if they have to be very crowded, because I have received a letter saying the factory closes on 1 May. My God! I don't know where those poor creatures can be put.

7. They have already been without work for a month and6 all their bread has to be paid for; I am tied up here by a thousand matters; I keep writing to beg the charity of devout people to help me. You cannot believe how this thought tears me apart, knowing that they are poor girls all rescued from danger, who are now so good. If they had to go back into danger, what would become of them!!

8. I have placed all my hopes in Mary Most Holy and Saint Anne to protect them. Help me, for pity's sake; send for them without delay, as suits you, in the large and small rooms, [saving them] from the snares of the world.7 This is what I desire; it [is] always a signal grace if you send for them in any way at all.

9. I trust so much in your charity that I shall obtain what I ask, and I beg you to give my respects to your most worthy sister, while I sign myself, full of esteem and gratitude, Your Lordship's

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

3 each = individually.

4 for sixty: L. 100 a month for 60 girls.

5 points: the points of the contract.

6 and have. And the Sisters have all the bread to pay for. The girls'

upkeep fell entirely on the Sisters.

7 Send for them without delay, when it suits you best, lodging them in the large and

small rooms already prepared, to free them from the dangers of the world.

1. So on Wednesday at 6 in the morning send Sr. A. Monaca and Sr. A. Evangelista2 third class; it costs 14 Lire each, that is 28 and some centesimi for the two.

3. Give them all the letters that have come for me; put them safely in their pockets so that they don't lose them.

4. If Father Fulgenzio has collected the money,6 give it to the Father.

Goodbye, your

5. Give the enclosed to the Father at once. I hope

those from Florence have arrived.

She gives instructions about the departure of two Sisters and about the house.

My daughter,

1. You did very well to go to the Archbishop, and the rest too. The Protector has died;2 you will have heard already; pray.

If you have no money I am sending you F. 20, and if you don't have enough for the one going to Foligno I shall send it. Oh! the Saint really does keep us in straitened circumstances!3

3. I have sent the Masses to the Chaplain.4 Listen, he wrote me a ferocious letter! Listen, take the sister out of the sacristy and put another there; for charity's sake don't upset him. Everything depends on him, do you understand?

4. I beg you, I commend Sr. A. Protasina to you: send her at once, and go to the station with them yourself; don't give them any money, I beg you. Do you understand? Goodbye. Oh, how much I have to do!5 Your

affect. M. R.
