She asks her to send a young woman to Imola and to ask a lady to try to find a job for Alessandro.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you Fr Peppi's letters, which you will read to that scatterbrain;1 then try to give her a dress costing a few pence, an old one if possible, and then at the sacrifice of F. 25 buy her a ticket to Imola and send her off at once, because I know she is doing immense harm; so send her.

2. See whether you could go to that sick lady2 to see if she would also do something for Alessandro, if he could have this job in Genoa; how much better that would be! Patience! Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 There is no information to check the persons named here or the facts.

2 There are no further details on this.

She asks for news of the hospital and asks her to write.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Last night I received your letter1 and hear you are still not well; I am truly sorry; for the rest, I could not understand anything you wrote.

2. I heard Fr Tito no longer wants you to pull teeth; is it true?2 How is that, do you have a dentist in the hospital? I cannot quite understand; write to me at the Rome address, because I shall go there next Monday,3 and then after 9 or 10 days I shall leave again to get nearer Piacenza.

Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 The letter has not been preserved.

2 One Sister had become skilled at pulling teeth.

3 Monday: 30 April.

The sacrifice of the missed meeting will make the next one far more joyful, inspiring and fruitful. She tells her of the opening of the new house in Naples and urges her to send the needy Sisters whatever they have to spare at Maratea.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Abraham's sacrifice made him Father of the living; so our sacrifice1 this time of not being able to see each other will mean that the first time we meet we shall stay together a long while and use all the time to pour out words all of God, and we shall speak of what the soul needs for its nourishment.

2. Oh! blessed day when I shall clasp my dear daughter to my heart. Oh! my God, how many expressions of love for You shall we be able to utter then?2 Both of us back from work and resting, yet always in the field, ready to undertake new battles and unparalleled labours, speaking of You, what can we say but that You are a beautiful and infinite love who have stolen everything from us and left us alone, exiles in a barren land, where so few know the language of Your love?3 Oh! daughter, when shall I see you all on fire, burning in these flames of love?

3. Listen, the house in this City4 is now being opened; so think of helping these poor sisters by sending them whatever you have to spare; do you understand? My God, we have still been unable to find anything; what a worry! Rent has to be paid, and you know what burdens I carry; for charity's sake, my daughter, send us something.

4. Listen, I leave for Rome on Monday; I am leaving Sr. A. Benedetta here for another five or 6 days5 and then she will join me in Rome. The Superior is Sr. A. Monica Balocchi, so address [things] to her; send nothing more to Rome.

5. I spoke with your Mayor and he has nothing against it as regards his daughter, so when you come you will bring her to me, won't you?6 It will certainly be early in July.

Goodbye, I am extremely busy; write and tell me everything without holding back. Your affectionate for ever

MOTHER Sr. A. R. G.

1 The Sister had longed for a meeting with the Mother not only for per-

sonal reasons but also to receive her directions for the new work.

M. Rosa places the sacrifice in the context of faith.

2 Outpourings of motherly and filial love, sublimated by their shared love of God,

who has called them both to follow Him.

3 Both of us back... love. An intense and stylistically elegant passage, though not

without emphasis. She addresses God, ending with a striking final question:

what else can we say but that You are a beautiful and infinite love...?

4 in Naples.

5 Monday, 30 April.

6 The Mayor of Maratea's daughter wanted to enter the Institute.

She has learned that, for lack of means, she is skimping on food. She urges her to buy food in the quantity and quality the community needs. The debts will be paid.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I hear from the teacher2 how short of means you are in this house and that only 2 soldi's worth of milk is bought for all the sisters. My God! how can you keep well? and you always with your inflamed bowels!!

2. Now I understand why; oh, for pity's sake, to pay off the debts you have run up3 you are economising far too much, even depriving yourself and the others of necessities; so stop such a bad way of going on at once and start buying meat and milk and wine in the quantity and quality a community of active people like you requires.4

3. So I hope you will do this at once, and we shall pay the debts, have no doubt. Listen, besides, you have an outside teacher, and so she goes and reports everything to the sisters; my God!

4. Listen, there is no longer any need to send or go to the Bishop; everything is settled.5

I await better news of your health, and remain your

Affect. M. R. P.S. I leave for Rome again tomorrow.

1 As with the other letters to her, the addressee is inferred from her

correspondence with the Mother.

2 A young lay teacher lived in community with the Sisters and was in

correspondence with the Mother.

3 She had run up debts buying furnishings needed for the house and the

chapel.

4 The Superior replied on 2 May, reassuring her about the milk and

food.

5 The Bishop of Novara, Mgr. Giacomo Filippo Gentile, had written to her

She gives news of the journey and of her health.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to keep my promise and give you news of the journey,2 which is not good, for I had such a bad headache that when I arrived I hardly knew whether I was alive.

2. Carla and Gaspare were at the station, but I could only say these words to them: "The little dress is from me and Sr. A. Benedetta sends you the pinafore".3 Oh! what suffering! I hope to be better tomorrow and shall write at greater length. Goodbye,

your affect. M.

Greet Father Agostino and the sisters for me.

1 It is dated 1 April, but is undoubtedly from 1 May. This is clear from

334,4.

2 news of the journey from Naples to Rome the day before.

3 La vestia e mi: perhaps the little dress (for the baby) is from me, the pinafore

A Sister will arrive; she is to meet her at the station. She is glad they have the little chapel in the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received yours1 and hear what you say about the sister you are expecting. So listen: as for the one who came down here, about whom they had written me so many vile things, it is not true; it was a slander, because they wanted to cover up for certain others by slandering her. God be blessed!

2. So I have decided to send her back to you, for the one who arrived does not seem to me as capable as this one. Anyway, one or the other, I shall send her on Thursday by the morning train; go and meet her at the station.

3. As for going to church, go; I see nothing against it; for the rest, I urge you to be brave and strong and very firm in observance.

4. You cannot believe how pleased I was to hear that you have the Chapel in the house.2 Oh, the goodness of God! So you are in your own house, on your own and away from lay people; blessed be the Lord!

Your affect. M. R.

1 Sr. A. Gesuina's letter is missing; there is, however, her reply of 7.5.77

to this letter.

2 The Chapel had been blessed on 14 April 1877.

She complains of the poor postal service. She urges her to take care of herself and avoid overtaxing her strength. Expressions of gratitude. Advice about the community and various news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just finished reading yours and have already telegraphed you; I don't know how it is, but I see letters are going astray, and so Sr. A. Santina did not receive yours, which contained the one I was addressing to the Father.

2. I also wrote at once to the Princess;1 I would like you to find out whether she received it. I have not yet seen her daughter, and not having the address of the inn I cannot even go there. Listen, I am registering this one because I see the Naples post is truly unreliable. Carla thanks you, and so does Gaspare; they will write to you.

3. My dear daughter, courage, it is time to toil to win a great crown;2 but I would not want you to suffer, since no one will be watching over you; so I fear you will tire yourself too much, and therefore I order you by holy obedience to take the greatest care of yourself. Do you understand? I assure you I see and hear you everywhere.

4. Oh! of course you have to deal with a mother who is not demonstrative and does not waste words on useless displays of affection; but in one word, my dear Benedetta, I tell you that the love I bear you is as great as the gratitude I owe you for having given such great help to my poor children!3 What do you think? You must know that this is in my mind above all else as the holiest duty I have, and I assure you there is nothing else that binds me so in gratitude.

5. Oh! never! never have I found a heart like yours, so great in charity towards me; so God alone could show you what I feel for you.

6. Listen, you did well not to accept that dinner from the Provincial,4 and it is not right for you to go there for meals any more; leave word with the sisters; and so, going (as I hope you are already in your own house),5 it is good that the sisters eat alone, because they keep silence and have reading; and Father Agostino apart, for you will tell him that in this way they will not take the liberty of admitting others to their table either, and that it is right for us to give them the example.6 With your ability you will show them that this is a good thing and that in this way you will see observance well established, for everything consists in that.

7. Tell Sr. A. Evangelista that I have received neither letter nor money, and tell the others they need not write, because I have already written to them. Sr. A. Evangelista is to write to him again. Do you understand?7

8. I have received the letters from Maratea,8 and you told me I would receive one from Father Agostino; tell him I have seen nothing.

Goodbye; many greetings to all the sisters, and receive an embrace from your

Affect. M. R.

Send me the address of the princess her daughter.9

1 To the Princess of Belmonte, Francesca Giuseppina Paolina Pignatelli

Aymeridi.

2 courage, it is time to toil. In her L of 3 May 1877 Sr. A. Benedetta had

described to her all her comings and goings from one palace of the Neapolitan nobility to another

to make known the work the FSA intended to do in nursing the

sick at home and to ask for their help in supporting it by sub-

scription and by spreading the word among influential acquaintances and friends.

3 She had been generous with financial and moral help to both Alessandro

and Carlotta.

4 This is the Provincial of the Minims of St Francis of Paola, Fr Giovanni Casals, who,

wanting to help the many poor of Naples, had asked Fr Agostino Donadio

to suggest a religious Congregation. He referred him to Mother Rosa and

arranged with her for her Sisters to be sent; at the start of the work they were lodg-

ed by the Fr Provincial himself.

5 ...so, going (as I hope you already are) to your own house, the little flat

reserved for you, it is good that the Sisters admit no one to their

meals, because they keep silence and there is reading.

6 and Fr Agostino... example. Not even Fr Agostino may be admitted;

tell him so... this will be an example of observance for the Sisters.

7 Sr. A. Evangelista Antoniazzi was expecting a letter with money from her

parish priest, but had not received it.

8 Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti and Sr. A. Irene Carmeli had written to her.

9 One of Princess Francesca's daughters was in Rome for a while.

Her mother had asked M. Rosa to visit her.

She is to accept the postulants and then bring them to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. Listen, gather postulants1 and then bring them to me in Piacenza, where I am going and where I shall expect you. Agreed? With the postulants: you will be their guide and come straight to Piacenza. Do as I say and, in haste, believe me

your affect. M. R.

1 Sr. A. Irene had already begun fruitful educational work among the girls in the boarding school, the school and the parish. "We have about a hundred girls to prepare for first communion", she wrote to M. Rosa on 30 April 1877. There were already some postulants in prospect. Cf. L 333, n. 6.

She invites her to come to Rome.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Here I am with you, answering your long letters;1 you will know well why I did not do so before: Carla was not well and gave me a great fright. Enough; thank the Lord she seems to have recovered.

2. Now to our business; listen, first of all I enclose two letters; read them, and then I would like you to be here by Friday, because I must leave on Saturday; they will manage.2

3. They have written to me from Maratea that every month they will be sent F. 40 and other provisions. So you see that little by little providence will come. Don't be dismayed.

4. Thank you for your ever dearer words; you will see that God will repay you well. My dear daughter, the love this mother of yours bears you is too great; you certainly cannot imagine it.

5. Listen, then, I shall expect you on Thursday by the 10 p.m. train. Come; much more in person. I am for ever your

affect. M. R.

1 The letters are dated 3 and 6 May.

2 Friday 11 May, because she was to leave on Saturday. The others, that is, the

Sisters, will manage on their own if they organise themselves well.

After postponing her departure she has not written again because of Carla's illness. She longs to have her near and urges her to look after herself and buy whatever the Sisters need.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. My silence in not writing to you after the telegram1 was because Carla got worse, and I leave you to imagine the state I was in; besides, a wet-nurse had to be found, and Gaspare left at once for the country... and I expect him back this evening with the wet-nurse. Now Carla is a little better but does nothing but cry because she cannot nurse the baby. Oh! what sorrow, my dear Sr. A. Benedetta.

2. Oh! how I have longed for you at my side! But that's how it is; we must make sacrifices and be patient; God wills it so. So our departure will be put off and I shall telegraph you.2

3. I would have a thousand things to tell you, but you can imagine, at Carla's bedside and always anxious!!

4. I hear so many good things from your letters of today and yesterday;3 I told you you would be consoled and receive fine alms! So yes, make the petition; it is better always to have; so make the petition.4

5. The sisters will reach you at once; one will come, and then I shall send you others or another.5

6. For charity's sake take care of yourself; remember you displease me if you don't, you grieve me, and I have too much grief already. For charity's sake buy what the sisters need; I have money for now. I want them to be well; leave them everything they need.

Goodbye; I want to post this soon. Your

Affect. M. R. 7. Be patient; you will hear everything in person.6

1 She had sent her the telegram to postpone her departure for Rome.

2 Sr. A. Benedetta had written asking her to postpone it, as her presence was

indispensable in Naples.

3 The two letters of 8 and 9 May. She had received gifts of money from vari-

ous noble persons and promises of help. They had also offered her various pieces of furniture for

the little flat in Palazzo Sannicandro, where they had lived since 8 May.

4 Make the petition, that is, the request to the Municipality for free premises for

the FSA work.

5 Sr. A. Benedetta had asked for more Sisters in addition to the first ones.

6 She must be patient if she sends no further news of herself and Carlotta.

Carla has been very ill but is now out of danger. Instructions on home nursing: the Sisters are not to walk long distances, and where the distance is great they are to stay several days in a row.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste, for you can well imagine the state of my head. Now I tell you: Carla was at death's door; now she is slowly improving but is out of danger; the wet-nurse was taken on, it was imprudent, she had a severe stabbing pain!1 Enough, now we are out of danger.2

2. I have already seen to the letters you write about; let us hope the Cardinal writes them.3 I won't write more, because I am in a hurry.

3. I never allow the sisters to walk where the distance is half an hour.4 When they are asked for, do as I do: ask for a carriage, otherwise they will wear themselves out. Do you understand? So I expect you to do the same.

4. Goodbye; if the distance is very great, it could be treated like the country, and then you can leave them three or four days, eating there.5 So they would sleep by day and stay up at night; or else, if it is a house of women only, they could take turns sleeping one night each; I think I have made myself clear. Goodbye, your

affect. M. R.

1 Carla had nearly died because of a very strong injection.

2 We are out of danger. Empathy makes her share fully in her daughter's illness and her joy

at the danger averted.

3 Sr. A. Benedetta had asked her to have the Cardinal Protector

Giuseppe Berardi write letters on behalf of the FSA: one to Cardinal Riario Sforza,

another to a Monsignor who was a benefactor.

4 To save money the Sisters preferred to walk long distances, to

the great detriment of their health. Sr. A. Benedetta was worried about it (cf. L 10 May) and

asked the Mother's advice.

5 ...if the distance... clear. Very wise and prudent arrangements.

They safeguarded the Rule and charity towards the Sisters and the neighbour they

served.

She sends her the letter for the Cardinal. A Sister will arrive to help the Superior, after which she can return to Rome.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I am sending you the letter1 and tell you it is something fine; I shall tell you in person why it is sealed. So take it to him at once.

2. Tomorrow I shall send you Sr. A. Speranza, who will do well for the subscription and be a help to the Superior.2 I would like to know how she is received and whether outsiders take to her. I hope the sisters will obey her. Won't they? So as soon as the sister has arrived, come here at once; I shall be expecting you.

3. As for the money, do as you think best; you know it is needed.3 So you decide. In haste, your

affect. M. R.

2 Sr. A. Speranza Volpini, together with Superior Monica Balocchi, was to

scriptions to the FSA and the corresponding offerings.

3 Providence had come through the generosity of the Neapolitan gentry.

Many, including the Cardinal, admiring the FSA's spirit of loving dedication,

had given generous gifts, in furniture and household goods as well as money,

enough to cover present needs with a good margin for the future.

Sr. A. Benedetta wanted to know whether she should bring some money with her to Rome.

She confirms the earlier news about Carlotta and Sr. A. Speranza. She expects her in Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your telegram and see you are worried about Carla. Now there is nothing more to fear, barring accidents.1 The little girl2 has her wet-nurse and is well.

2. You cannot believe how painful your absence is to me, but patience, God willed it so!

3. But I hope Sr. A. Speranza will be very well received, and you will see that with the Princess and all the others too she will do [well].3 Urge the Superior to get on with her and let them give a good example, so that everyone must admire them and marvel.4

4. I hope you have received the Cardinal's letter and taken it to the Card.5

5. Listen, I hope to see you soon; so on Thursday6 I shall have you met off the 10 p.m. train, and then in person [...]. Try to bring me a little money.7 Goodbye, your

2 The baby, Maria Adelaide.

3 will do well. Cf. L 342,2.

4 They must give a shining witness of love and harmony, such as to

She encourages her not to worry, as everything has been cleared up and nothing more will happen.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter with Fr Accinelli's. Don't worry; I hope you have received a letter of mine telling you how to proceed.1

2. So courage; it is all over, and I hope nothing more will happen.2 Humility, daughter, and you will have everything.

Goodbye, I am in a hurry, your

affect. M. R.

3. P.S. I have just received your other letter; I tell you not to worry,

it is all over; be resigned and you will see that you will be content. Goodbye.

1 This is L 326.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received two letters from you and am replying to you. I hear there is a piano for sale at F. 100.1 See whether they would let it go for a little less and buy it at once; then a lesson every fortnight will do, and you will see it is enough.2

2. I would not want you to do anything foolish with that family3 to make them notice it; I hope not, and soon I shall hear you play well. Goodbye, your, I am in a hurry, your

My dear Father Agostino,

1. Sr. A. Benedetta arrived safely last night, and I hear she is needed back. So she will be there again tomorrow;1 when I leave she too will leave for Naples and stay there as long as she sees there is need.

2. So I have decided, and you will see you will be pleased.2

3. My Father, rest assured that the Saint loves you and [has] already numbered you among her dear sons;3 I shall write to you in due course; I am leaving. Your

Affect. Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Will be there again: she means there, in Naples. She too was to leave.

2 You will be pleased. Fr Agostino was busy helping Sr. A. Benedetta and the

the one at Maratea.

She informs her of her itinerary of visits to the communities.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Although I haven't a moment to breathe, I am writing to you, and I telegraphed you today. So tomorrow morning at 8 I go to S. Martinello1 and spend the whole day there, and then the next day I go straight on to Gualdo Tadino,2 where I shall stay one day, and leave again for Appignano,3 God willing.

2. I hope to find letters from you, which I so much want; write to me at once. For charity's sake, be cheerful. Carla had a good journey, and they telegraphed me that she is well.

Goodbye, ever your

Affect. M. R. G.

1 S. Martinello, near Perugia.

2 Gualdo Tadino (PG). Three Sisters nursed the patients in the small

hospital.

She has had no news. She urges her to look after herself and be cheerful at the thought that they will soon meet.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am at S. Martinello, and from here too a line to my dear Benedetta, for it seems a century since I had you.1 Enough, let us hope it will be short2 and I hope to see you again. I don't know what to say; being without news makes me feel I am at the end of the world. Dear Jesus, [what] pain!

2. What is Fr Agostino doing? Give him my warm regards; and you, take care of yourself and be cheerful.

3. Remember we shall see each other again, and full of consolation at having laboured for God, we shall tell each other of the fine days of suffering, drawing from them our greatest consolation.3

4. Suffering, you are the herald of eternal joy!4 What a beautiful thought! Goodbye.

Your affect. M. R.

5. Tomorrow at 5 p.m. I hurry on to Gualdo Tadino.

1 Since I had you at my side.

2 that the time apart may be short.

3 Full of consolation at having spent our energies for the Lord, we shall tell

each other of difficulties, pains and hardships faced and overcome, drawing from them our

greatest consolation, which is a ground of hope and greater trust in God.

4 Suffering: sufferings borne and offered are the announcement (herald) and promise of

endless joy to come.

My daughter,

1. I forgot to take Clelia's uniform, that is, the hat and the little cape.2 Be sure not to forget it; look carefully.

2. Goodbye; tomorrow I shall be at Gualdo Tadino all day and leave again on Wednesday evening.3 Goodbye, your

She is travelling and so cannot send the Superior to Naples.
